extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, policy researchers, rulemaking practitioners, and public-interest advocates organizing or evaluating mass comment campaigns
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and designing mass comment campaigns in agency rulemaking — what makes an individual comment within a mass campaign be treated as 'substantive' and how agencies respond to organized volumes of similar input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Has unique sentences (not 100% template)
rubrics_metrics.description: A substantive mass comment includes unique sentences and is not 100% identical to the campaign's template.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balla finds that form letters that are not verbatim duplicates are more likely to be treated as substantive. Even small departures from the template (unique sentences) increase the chance the agency will address the comment's points. Anti-pattern: comments that are exact copies are often deduplicated or ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Includes a specific personal example
rubrics_metrics.description: The comment contains at least one sentence describing a personal experience or individualized context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: a single sentence with personal experience increases likelihood of being treated as substantive. Personalization signals distinctness and relevance to the agency's factual record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cites unique data point or study
rubrics_metrics.description: The comment cites a specific data point, study, or empirical evidence not present in the template.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments that introduce novel factual or analytical claims supported by citations are more likely to be addressed than pure expressions of preference. Providing evidence makes the comment more actionable for agency consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggests a specific implementation alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: The comment proposes a concrete, specific alternative way to implement, revise, or interpret a proposed rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies are more likely to respond to comments that offer specific alternatives or implementation details rather than only stating support or opposition. Specificity helps agencies evaluate practicability and legal consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addresses one of the agency's stated questions
rubrics_metrics.description: The comment directly responds to a question or request for information posed in the agency's notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targeted responses to the agency's stated questions are more likely to be treated as relevant and substantive. Aligning comment content with the notice's issues improves the chance of engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure-template mass comment (identical)
rubrics_metrics.description: A comment that is 100% identical to thousands of others and merely repeats the campaign text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the canonical anti-pattern: identical, template-only comments tend to be counted together and are unlikely to move the agency because they add no new factual or legal content. Agencies face deduplication pressures and may treat these as expressions rather than substantive input.

rubrics_metrics.name: States only support or opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: A comment whose entire content is simply 'support' or 'oppose' without engaging provisions or reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements of preference without reasons or evidence fare poorly. Agencies generally prioritize comments that engage with specific provisions, legal rationale, or factual claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: No engagement with specific provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The comment fails to reference or analyze particular regulatory text, provisions, or potential effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments that do not engage with specific provisions are less useful for agencies drafting responses or revising rules. Effective comments cite sections, explain impacts, or identify errors in proposed regulatory language.

rubrics_metrics.name: No personal context
rubrics_metrics.description: The comment lacks any individualized context that would distinguish it from mass-produced text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of personal or situational context reduces a comment's distinctiveness and persuasiveness. Even minimal personalization can increase perceived substantive value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical volume counted together but limited influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies typically aggregate mass comments and numerical volume does not translate proportionally to influence on outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balla finds that agencies 'count mass comments together and respond to the substantive points raised' — volume matters less than whether the campaign introduces new substantive arguments. Campaign designers should prioritize novelty and substance over pure numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form letters with novel substantive arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Form-letter campaigns that incorporate novel substantive arguments (not just template text) are more likely to be addressed than truly identical text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A campaign can be effective when templates are modified to include substantive claims or evidence. The presence of new legal, factual, or analytic points within form letters raises their salience for agency reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency procedural challenges: deduplication and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies face procedural burdens in deduplicating, organizing, and substantively analyzing mass comment inflows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These resource constraints influence how comments are processed and can lead to mechanical deduplication or selective substantive review. Recognize that agencies may not have capacity to deeply analyze thousands of similar submissions, which affects campaign strategy and realistic expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass campaigns can crowd out individual substantive comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-scale organized campaigns may consume agency processing resources and thereby reduce attention to separate individual substantive comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balla notes a potential negative externality: mass campaigns can inadvertently 'crowd out' distinct, detailed comments. Campaign organizers should weigh this trade-off and consider strategies that preserve space for high-quality individual input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective engagement: agencies respond to substantive points
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies selectively engage with and respond to substantive arguments within the mass comment stream rather than treating each comment individually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies tend to identify and address recurring substantive points raised across submissions. Repetition of the same substantive argument (even across many comments) signals importance, but exact-duplicate repetition without novelty is unlikely to change deliberations.
